elements.quote: We updated a living systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate the extent of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in schools.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review and meta-analysis.

elements.quote: We updated a living systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate the extent of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in schools.
elements.reason: The abstract states the objective of the review.

elements.quote: In this update we modified our inclusion criteria to include: 1) cohort studies; 2) cross-sectional studies that investigated and cross-assessed SARS-COV-2 positivity rates in schools and communities; and 3) pre-post studies.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the main inclusion criteria.

elements.quote: We performed a meta-analysis on nine of the 11 cohort studies investigating IAR in schools.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to synthesize the results (meta-analysis).

elements.quote: In total from the two updates and using the new inclusion criteria, we identified 11 cohort studies (1 st update: n = 5; 2 nd update: n = 6) and one cross-sectional study (1 st update: n = 1; 2 nd update: n = 0).
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies.

elements.quote: Nine cohort studies reported a total of 91 student and 52 staff index cases that exposed 5698 contacts with 101 secondary infections
elements.reason: The abstract reports results for the main outcomes, including the number of studies and participants (contacts/cases).

elements.quote: Nine cohort studies reported a total of 91 student and 52 staff index cases that exposed 5698 contacts with 101 secondary infections (overall infection attack rate (IAR) = 1.45%, 95% CI = 0.31%-3.26%). IARs for students and school staff were 1.66% (95% CI = 0.08%-4.78%) and 1.18% (95% CI = 0.00%-4.43%) respectively.
elements.reason: The abstract reports summary estimates and confidence intervals for the meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Higher IAR were found in students, compared to staff.
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect when comparing groups.

elements.quote: The risk of bias was found to be high for most studies identified, limiting the confidence in results.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes important limitations (risk of bias).

elements.quote: There is limited high-quality evidence available to quantify the extent of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in schools or to compare it to community transmission. Emerging evidence suggests the overall IAR and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate in school settings are low.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide the register name and registration number.

elements.quote: The results from cohort and cross-sectional studies found that the overall IAR and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate in school settings are low . Our previous review suggested lower IAR and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate in students compared to school staff [4], whereas in this update when we combined studies from the second and first update we found higher IAR in students when compared to school staff. ... However, there is uncertainty about which grade school children are more likely susceptible to and transmit SARS-CoV-2 in schools.
elements.reason: The text describes the current state of knowledge regarding SARS-CoV-2 transmission in schools (low IAR/positivity rates, conflicting findings on student vs. staff susceptibility) and explicitly identifies uncertainties regarding susceptibility by grade level.

elements.quote: The main strength of this living systematic review is that it estimates pooled IARs and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates for students and school staff, and it is updated with new studies to re-evaluate the conclusions given the rapid pace of ongoing research, to investigate the rate of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in schools.
elements.reason: The text explains the need for the review: to provide updated estimates of transmission rates in the context of rapidly evolving research to aid understanding of transmission risk.

elements.quote: The main strength of this living systematic review is that it estimates pooled IARs and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates for students and school staff, and it is updated with new studies to re-evaluate the conclusions given the rapid pace of ongoing research
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly identifies itself as an updated living systematic review and explains the need for the update (to re-evaluate conclusions given the rapid pace of ongoing research).

This is a systematic review of observational studies (cohort and cross-sectional) regarding transmission rates, not a review of intervention effects (e.g., a clinical trial of a drug or therapy), so a mechanism of action is not applicable.
The review focuses on observational data regarding transmission rates rather than evaluating a complex intervention or delivery context requiring a logic model.

elements.quote: We updated a living systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate the extent of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in schools.
elements.reason: The review explicitly states its objective to investigate the extent of SARS-CoV-2 transmission in schools.

This is a review of observational studies (cohort and cross-sectional) investigating transmission rates, not a review of intervention effects (e.g., randomized controlled trials of a specific treatment or intervention), so PICO comparisons are not applicable.

elements.quote: We included children (defined as ≤18 years old) who were attending school, and their close contacts (family and household members, teachers, school support staff). We excluded home-schooled children and their close contacts, and schools with student numbers below 20. For study outcomes, we included infections traced to a school index case with a COVID-19 positive test. We updated inclusion criteria of study types to include: 1) Cohort studies... 2) Cross-sectional studies... 3) Pre-post studies... We excluded household studies unless specifically linked to school outbreaks; and studies where rates are measured in schools and without comparison of community rates.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly defines the population (children ≤18, contacts), settings (schools), and study designs (cohort, cross-sectional, pre-post) used for eligibility.

elements.quote: We included articles in peer-reviewed journals and pre-prints, and excluded comments, conference abstracts and interviews.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the publication status (peer-reviewed journals and pre-prints) and report types (excluding comments, conference abstracts, and interviews) for eligibility.
The review does not report excluding studies specifically because outcomes were not measured versus not reported; this is not a relevant distinction for the eligibility criteria described.

elements.quote: We found 11 cohort studies [13-17,24-29] that investigated secondary infection attack ( Table 1 and Table 2 ) and one cross-sectional studies [18] that investigated SARS-CoV-2 positivity compared to community rates ( Table 3 and Table 4 ).

elements.quote: For cohort studies, all studies were at risk of selection bias to varying degrees. Although most studies performed well in terms of representativeness of the exposed group in the school, all but one performed poorly for representativeness of the unexposed groups, and no studies confirmed that the outcomes were not present at the start of the study. Comparability was reasonable across all studies with most schools matched for NPI measures and participants matched for age. Ten studies were at high risk of detection bias caused by differences in screening or testing or both, and 9 of 11 studies were at high risk of attrition bias with loss-to-follow up more than 20% or not described in the 14-day follow-up period
